name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review (TAR) are methods for classifying large sets of documents in e-discovery using machine learning, usually to decide which items are responsive to a request or protected by privilege. The scope covers the whole review pipeline, from collection and processing through to production, and it applies wherever the volume of documents makes manual review impractical. These techniques sit inside e-discovery and large-scale document analysis, and they are used in litigation, investigations, regulatory responses and internal audits. The aim is not to remove human judgment but to direct it to the documents that matter most.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review (TAR) are methods for classifying large sets of documents in e-discovery using machine learning, usually to decide which items are responsive to a request or protected by privilege. The scope covers the whole review pipeline, from collection and processing through to production, and it applies wherever the volume of documents makes manual review impractical. These techniques sit inside e-discovery and large-scale document analysis, and they are used in litigation, investigations, regulatory responses and internal audits. The aim is not to remove human judgment but to direct it to the documents that matter most.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: TAR runs on document review platforms that combine storage, indexing, search and machine learning components, often deployed in the cloud or on dedicated servers. The underlying infrastructure includes compute for training and inference, secure storage for document images and extracted text, and audit logs that record every action. Many platforms support active learning, where the model updates as reviewers code documents, and they may integrate with analytics for near-duplicate detection and email threading. Access controls, encryption and data residency options are part of the setup because the material is often sensitive or privileged.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with processing and deduplication, followed by a seed set of documents coded by human reviewers to train a classifier. The model then ranks or scores the remaining documents, and reviewers examine samples to measure precision and recall, often using an elusion test to check for missed relevant items. In continuous active learning, the model retrains as reviewers code the highest-ranked documents, which can reduce the total review effort. Throughout, teams keep records of the training data, model versions and sampling results so the process can be explained and defended later.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in TAR turn on proportionality, defensibility and transparency, and courts may require parties to disclose how the method works and how quality was measured. Provenance matters: teams typically document the chain of custody, the training and validation sets, the model version and the sampling protocol, because these records support the reliability of the review. Privilege and privacy risks remain, especially when documents cross borders or contain personal data, and errors can lead to waiver or sanctions. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 29 AI case law precedents are useful references for how these issues have been treated in practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Predictive coding is moving toward tighter integration with large language models, which can assist with summarization, issue tagging and privilege review, though the core classification task still relies on validated workflows. Expect more hybrid approaches that combine active learning with generative models, and more attention to explainability and model monitoring as regulators and courts ask harder questions. The volume of AI-related litigation and regulation, including the 148 active AI lawsuits and 6978 state AI bills tracked on this site, suggests that scrutiny of automated review will only increase. Smaller, more focused review sets and continuous quality checks are likely to become standard as compute costs and data volumes both rise.
